# FLOID — Full Product Reference

> Free design process scheduling software for industrial designers and product development teams.

Website: https://floid.design/
Pricing: Free (no account required, no usage limits)
Platform: Web browser — works on desktop and tablet
Category: Project scheduling, timeline management, product development planning

---

## Overview

FLOID is a free, browser-based timeline scheduling tool designed specifically for industrial designers and product development teams. It provides a visual timeline interface for planning projects with multiple parallel schedule tracks, drag-and-drop phases, tasks, and milestones.

Unlike general-purpose project management tools, FLOID is focused on the scheduling needs of physical product development — where teams need to coordinate multiple workstreams (engineering, tooling, prototyping, testing, regulatory) against a master timeline.

---

## Detailed Features

### Timeline Scheduling
- Visual drag-and-drop timeline with phases, tasks, and milestones
- Resize phases and tasks by dragging edges
- Zoom in/out to adjust timeline granularity
- Scroll and navigate large timelines fluidly

### Multiple Schedule Sections
- Create multiple schedule tracks (sections) within a single project
- Each section has its own set of phases, tasks, and milestones
- Color-code sections for visual organization
- Collapse or expand sections to manage complexity

### Master Schedule Sync
- Designate one section as the master schedule
- Other sections can be "locked" to sync their date range with the master
- Or set sections to "independent" mode to maintain their own dates
- When the master schedule changes, locked sections automatically rescale

### Phases, Tasks, and Milestones
- Phases are top-level timeline blocks with duration
- Tasks are sub-items within phases, also with duration
- Milestones are single-point markers (no duration) for key dates and deadlines
- All items use relative positioning — resizing a parent cascades to children

### Export and Sharing
- Export individual schedules as .floid files to share with collaborators
- Export full project backups as .floid-project files
- Export timeline as an image
- Import .floid files to bring in schedules from other projects

### User Experience
- Dark mode support (follows system preference)
- Keyboard shortcuts for common actions
- Double-click to rename items inline
- Drag to rearrange sections
- Right-click context menus
- Clean, minimal interface designed to stay out of your way

---

## Use Cases

### Product Development Timeline Planning
Plan the full lifecycle of a physical product — from concept through production. Create parallel tracks for industrial design, mechanical engineering, tooling, and regulatory, all synced to a master schedule.

### Multi-Workstream Coordination
When multiple teams or disciplines need to work in parallel, FLOID's section-based timeline lets you visualize how workstreams align and where handoffs occur.

### Schedule Sharing and Review
Export individual schedules as .floid files to share with stakeholders or collaborators who also use FLOID. Export timeline images for presentations and status updates.

### Quick Project Estimation
Rapidly sketch out a project timeline to estimate duration and identify scheduling conflicts before committing to a detailed plan.

---

## Comparison to Other Tools

### FLOID vs. General Project Management Tools (Asana, Monday, Jira)
FLOID is focused purely on visual timeline scheduling. It does not include task assignment, communication, or workflow automation. This makes it faster and simpler for teams that just need to plan and visualize a schedule without the overhead of a full project management platform.

### FLOID vs. Gantt Chart Software (Microsoft Project, TeamGantt)
FLOID's timeline model is simpler than traditional Gantt charts. It uses relative positioning instead of rigid date dependencies, which makes it easier to quickly sketch and adjust timelines. It also supports multiple independent schedule sections in a single view, which is uncommon in Gantt tools.

### FLOID vs. Spreadsheet-Based Scheduling
Many teams use Excel or Google Sheets for scheduling. FLOID provides the same visual timeline layout but with drag-and-drop interaction, automatic date calculation, and proper export formats — without the manual formatting work.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is FLOID free?
Yes. FLOID is completely free to use with no account required and no usage limits.

### Do I need to create an account?
No. FLOID runs entirely in your browser. No sign-up, no login, no account needed.

### What platforms does FLOID support?
FLOID runs in any modern web browser on desktop or tablet. There is no native mobile app, but the web app works on tablet-sized screens.

### Can I share schedules with my team?
Yes. Export a schedule as a .floid file and share it with anyone. They can import it into their own FLOID instance. You can also export timeline images for presentations.

### Is FLOID good for industrial design projects?
Yes — FLOID was built specifically for industrial designers and product development teams. Its multi-section timeline model matches how physical product development projects are typically structured, with parallel workstreams for design, engineering, tooling, testing, and regulatory.

### Can I use FLOID for software projects?
While FLOID was designed for physical product development, its timeline scheduling features work for any type of project that benefits from visual timeline planning.

### Does FLOID support Gantt chart dependencies?
FLOID uses a relative positioning model rather than rigid task dependencies. This makes timelines more flexible and easier to adjust, but it means there are no automatic dependency arrows between tasks.

### Where is my data stored?
Your project data stays in your browser. FLOID does not send your data to any server.

### Can I export my timeline as an image?
Yes. FLOID supports exporting your timeline view as an image file, useful for presentations and status reports.

---

## Technical Details

- Built with React and TypeScript
- Client-side only — no server, no database, no data collection
- Uses local browser storage
- Lightweight and fast — no heavy frameworks or dependencies
- Works offline after initial load
